title: Starting trombone in 1921 despite his father's wish, and the fear of tasting brass
summary: Clark began trombone about 1921, over his mother's objection. His teacher said solid-brass instruments were never harmful, and Clark was taught to breathe from the corner of his mouth.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: What year did you start playing an instrument?

My mother didn't want me to do it but after she saw that I was just headlong to do it, she said, well you're grown now and I can't tell you what to do. But that's your father's wish for you never to play a wind instrument. Why don't you play a string instrument? I told her that I don't like a string instrument.

After I'd taken it up, I really wanted it. So I talked to my teacher, the man that taught me. And he knew my father. And I asked him about it. He says, well, I'll tell you, in the days that your father started and I started, they didn't make anything but solid brass instruments. They didn't play them like they do now. He says, you don't have to worry about tasting brass. If you would happen to take sick or anything, or inhaling that, drawing your breath from that brass, you'd never feel because that brass, that instrument is coated in and out. You see, in those days all the instruments were brass, solid brass. It wasn't coated like they are now. See, because I can remember way back, there used to be a bass player around here by the name of Pierre, had an upright bass, what they called a monster. It was an E flap but it was a big one. And it had a bell almost as big as a bell of mine. They used to call it the monster E. And it was solid brass. And when he shined that thing you could look at it if he walked in the sun.
And what does tasting that brass do to you?

Well you just taste it all the time when you cough. You know you have a cough and you taste it. Because my mother told me, my father used to tell her, every time he coughed, nor I tasted brass. But things have changed now.
I just wondered if it would have gotten your blood or if it got your tongue off?

No, in some kind of way it gets into your Bronicle II, some kind of way down in there, I don't know. You see, but I was taught never to breathe in an instrument. When you take your breath, I was taught to take my breath from the corner of my mouth. Never take your breath right from the instrument. I always take my breath from the corner of my mouth. I was taught that.
